[PATH:empirical] Administrative matched employer-employee panel data (e.g., LEHD in the U.S. or IAB in Germany) linked to regional R&D intensity measures — Such data allow direct estimation of job tenure, churn rates, and employment transitions for native workers in non-tradable service sectors, before and after high-skilled immigration shocks, with regional variation in R&D intensity to test the hypothesized conditional effect.

[PATH:literature] Survey of regional labor market adjustment mechanisms (e.g., job displacement, occupational mobility) from the economics literature on immigration and local labor markets — Existing studies (e.g., Peri & Sparber, Dustmann et al.) suggest high-skilled immigration may reallocate native workers toward communication-intensive or service roles, but rarely examine churn and tenure in non-tradable sectors specifically in low-R&D regions. A systematic review could identify whether the hypothesized mechanism is supported or contradicted by prior evidence.

[PATH:theoretical] Computable general equilibrium (CGE) or search-and-matching model calibrated to a low-R&D regional economy — A formal model can isolate the causal channels: if high-skilled immigrants increase local demand for non-tradable services, native workers may experience higher turnover due to job competition or skill mismatch. Simulating the model under different R&D intensities can provide theoretical confirmation or refutation of the hypothesized effect.

scope.domain: labor economics, regional wage dynamics, job stability
